problem: Wheelchair-mounted single-arm manipulators cannot do bimanual ADLs (opening a jar, pouring, lifting a tray), and adding a second arm to the chair costs weight, power and space. Existing bimanual and base-placement methods assume a jointly planned, calibrated fixed workspace, not a second mobile arm that must complement an already-committed anchor grasp.
motivation: An on-demand mobile manipulator could supply the second hand and then leave, but it must decide where to stand and what to grasp given the anchor's fixed grasp, so that the user can teleoperate it intuitively. Task semantics (which part to grasp, how it will move) are needed, while 3D geometry should stay with geometric tools.
key_idea: Bimanual joining is decomposed into plan (VLM infers target and motion vectors), drive (base pose scored by wheelchair-referenced opposition), and grasp (candidates ranked by task-conditioned directional manipulability).
insight: The VLM is used only for task-level reasoning (mode, target pixel, motion type and direction), while all 3D quantities are computed geometrically. This lets the complement pick grasps that are dexterous along the task motion. The gains show up on different-object tasks (stir 4/5 vs 2/5, pour 5/5 vs 3/5) and in reduced operator grasp-correction time. There are no component ablations, so the necessity of each scoring term is not shown.
method: Phase 1 (plan): Gemini Robotics-ER 1.6 receives the head-camera image and task text and returns, in one call, the mode (same/different object), a target grasp pixel and description, a motion type (5 classes), a camera-frame linear direction and an angular axis. The 3D target comes from depth at the target pixel.
Phase 2 (drive): candidate base poses are sampled on a discretized SE(2) grid around the target, keeping only collision-free ones. Each is scored as S = 0.30*S_d + 0.35*S_o,ee + 0.35*S_o,base.
Distance term S_d: a Gaussian on complement-to-target distance centered at 0.6 m with sigma 0.2 m, the middle of Stretch's reach.

Opposition terms: S_o,ee is the cosine similarity that makes the complement gripper approach from the side opposite the anchor gripper. S_o,base is the cosine similarity between the base-to-target vector and the anchor's base-to-target vector mirrored across the anchor's forward axis.

Phase 3 (grasp) sampling: after driving, a close-range RGB-D view is captured and the VLM refines the grasp pixel. 64 Fibonacci-sphere approach directions times 4 rolls are sampled, then filtered by a simplified gripper collision check against the point cloud and by IK feasibility.

Phase 3 (grasp) ranking: candidates are scored by directional manipulability along the VLM's linear and angular directions. The linear and rotational Jacobian parts are weighted by motion type (e.g. 1.0/0 for linear, 0.5/0.5 for balanced). The score is multiplied by a runway penalty tanh(time-to-joint-limit/1 s), and the argmax is executed.

setting.backbone: Gemini Robotics-ER 1.6 (frozen VLM) plus geometric tools (Pinocchio kinematics, Jacobian manipulability)
setting.observation: Head-camera RGB-D on the Stretch 3, with a wide-angle view at the summon pose and a close-range arm-camera RGB-D view with point cloud
setting.action_space: SE(2) base pose selected from a sampled grid, then 6-DoF gripper grasp pose, followed by expert teleoperation with a SpaceMouse for the collaborative motion
setting.privileged: Anchor grasp pose and anchor base pose are known; a predefined summon location is used; the human expert teleoperator adjusts the grasp and executes the task motion

numbers_note: Real-robot manipulation paper with no standard embodied-navigation benchmark; results are 5 trials per task on 4 tabletop tasks. Overall success is JOIN 19/20, AnyGrasp 14/20, Teleop 20/20. Per-task success for JOIN: box lift 5/5, bottle open 5/5, stir pot 4/5, pour 5/5. Times are in the paper's Table 1.
results: JOIN succeeds in 19/20 real-robot trials, close to full teleoperation (20/20) and above the AnyGrasp+SAM3 baseline (14/20). It also cuts operator grasp-adjustment time (e.g. 11 vs 38 s on stirring, 15 vs 34 s on box lift). Full teleoperation remains faster in total task time on every task.
limitations: Only 5 trials per cell, four tabletop tasks, one apartment environment, and a single expert teleoperator who is a paper author. There are no ablations or user study, and only single-step joining is addressed.
The complement still needs a predefined summon location, static hand-set scoring weights, and operator teleoperation for the collaborative motion; it remains slower than full teleoperation.
